subject: research/selfrep-redesign
professional: a design-for-manufacture / open-hardware engineer who has built RepRap-class machines and published on self-replicating manufacturing (the reviewer of a Robotica or Journal of Mechanical Design paper on replication closure). They would check first: that the part list and the vitamin/makeable split follow a cited bill of materials, that the penalty budget is tied to something measurable (stiffness, wear, failure), that the closure metric cannot be moved by an accounting choice, and what the result adds beyond the known RepRap printed-bushing and printed-nut variants.

evidence.correctness: Ran `python3 experiments/run.py`: output is byte-identical to the committed experiments/results.txt (diff empty), so the numbers are reproducible. Independently recomputed with a scratch script (/tmp/claude-0/s2/ind.py, run with python3 -I, using only the BOM data from selfrep-closure and my own makeable test, not selfrep_redesign): (1) baseline 51 lines, 29 vitamin lines, closure lines 43.1%, mass 22.4%, cost 15.9% (script prints 0.4314 / 0.2241 / 0.1586), matching README. (2) All seven substitutions applied: 19 vitamin lines, 60.4% / 35.8% / 47.7%, matching README. (3) Greedy vs exhaustive: counted rows by eye from results.txt, 4 of 21 differ (lines 3.0, mass 1.0, mass 2.0, cost 2.0), so 17 of 21 matches, and the largest gap 28.6 vs 26.1 = 2.5, as stated. The arithmetic is right. But a number a reader would act on is moved by an accounting choice: _printed() gives every replacement part cost 0.5 per unit, while the purchased M8 nut it replaces costs 0.03 per unit. In my script, replacing only the M8 nut gives cost closure 33.6% (the README's budget-0.5 figure); if the printed nut is costed at the 0.03 it replaces, the same swap gives 17.4%. So about 16 of the 17.7 points of the headline cost-closure jump come from making a 3-unit line into a 50-unit line and counting all of it as makeable. Reading code and recomputing the arithmetic only: not 3 because the headline cost finding is an artefact.
evidence.completeness: Claims in README checked: seven substitutions in design.py (present, 7 entries); exhaustive over 2^7 subsets (present, exhaustive()); greedy gain-per-penalty (present); random baseline of 8 evaluations, mean of 200 runs (present, run.py); 500-draw penalty sensitivity (present, run.py); tests `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v` gives 5 tests (ran: 5 pass); results.txt, figure.py and cost_closure.svg exist. All stated outputs are produced end to end. Not exercised: the live page https://marisstella.app/research/selfrep-redesign/ (not loaded). Not done and honestly declared: no mechanical model, no LLM proposer. No TODOs or stubs found. The `Owner steps` (print and test) are not done, by design.
evidence.verification: Ran `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`: 5 tests, 5 pass (pytest not needed; stdlib). Seeded two mutations in src/selfrep_redesign/design.py, each reverted with `git checkout` (git status clean for the project afterwards). Mutation A, exhaustive() budget test `penalty(c) <= budget` changed to `<= budget + 0.5`: 2 tests failed (budget respected, zero budget). Caught. Mutation B, greedy() ranking `g / SUBS[i].penalty` changed to `g * SUBS[i].penalty` (picks the worst gain-per-penalty instead of the best, the rule the README names): 5 of 5 pass, nothing failed. Not caught. The greedy test only asserts that greedy is within budget and not better than exhaustive, which any rule satisfies. No test pins any number in results.txt, the cost-closure value, the printed-part cost, or the sensitivity routine (which lives in run.py and has no test). Score 2: the core optimiser budget logic is guarded but a changed headline method is not.
evidence.craft: Read design.py (106 lines), tests/test_redesign.py, experiments/run.py and the selfrep-closure files it imports (closure.py, bom.py). Defects: (1) import by `sys.path.insert` of a sibling project's src tree, so the package cannot be installed from its own pyproject (dependencies = []), and pyproject lists a package that fails to import outside the monorepo; (2) run.py mutates the module-global SUBS list in place for the sensitivity loop, and rebuilds it each draw; fragile and untested; (3) closure_of() reimplements closure() from selfrep-closure (a copied engine; the test only checks they agree at one point); (4) _printed() hard-codes cost 0.5 for any printed replacement, the source of the cost artefact above; (5) penalty is a bare additive float and substitutions that overlap (printed-bushings and printed-idlers both touch bearings) are treated as independent; (6) no input validation (an unknown index raises IndexError); (7) the SVG figure is regenerated by figure.py, not checked. Short, readable and with honest ASSUMPTION comments, but a senior reviewer would ask for a package boundary and a test for every reported statistic.
evidence.claims: Checked each README result against results.txt and my recomputation: baseline 43.1/22.4/15.9 and 29 lines (true); all substitutions 60.4/35.8/47.7 (true); 'mass closure stays below 36%' (35.8, true); 'greedy matched exhaustive in 17 of 21 rows, at most 2.5 points short' (true); 'random 0 to 16 points below' (true, max 16.4 in cost at 0.5); sensitivity 'no set above 13%' and 'top five about half' (13.0 and 52.2%, true, and all five contain wood-smooth-rods and printed-m8-nuts, true). False or unbacked: 'Cost closure responds much more than mass ... because nuts and bearings are many cheap lines' is not the reason; the response is mostly because a printed nut is costed at 0.5 each against 0.03 for the purchased nut (see correctness), which the README never states. The dowel rod is assigned 30 g against 140 to 165 g for the steel rod it replaces; if the dowel is given the steel mass the budget-1.0 mass closure is 37.0% against 28.6%, so the 'rises only to 28.6%' statement depends on an unstated mass assumption. Disclosure that results are assumed and simulated only is present and strong; the claim that this is 'follow-up' work cites only one sibling project and one paper.
evidence.fitness: Could a researcher build on it? The code and the sibling BOM are open and the loop is easy to rerun with different penalties, which is useful. But the penalties, replacement masses and replacement costs are the author's own, there is no model that connects a substitution to function, and the 2^7 search is trivially solved by enumeration (the README says so), so the greedy and random comparisons carry no information about larger spaces. A researcher would have to replace every input before using any conclusion. This is a worked toy, not a programme step: the directory is not listed in research/PROGRAMMES.md, so it falls below the PhD-level programme bar in research/CLAUDE.md. A hobbyist could use it to see which BOM lines dominate; they could not use it to decide what to print.
evidence.domain: Nearest prior work: the RepRap project itself (Jones et al., Robotica 2011, cited), the long-standing community variants of printed bushings, printed nuts and wooden or printed frames (RepRap Darwin and Mendel parts lists, 'printable' replacements), and the replication-closure literature (Moses and Chirikjian on robotic self-replication; Freitas and Merkle, Kinematic Self-Replicating Machines, 2004, which separate material, part and system closure). None of the latter two is cited. The question 'which substitutions cut vitamins under a budget' is reasonable, but the answer is determined by the author's list and penalties and by the count-weighting of box-size fastener lines; a replication-closure specialist would say the result is a restatement of the input assumptions (the biggest gains are the lines with the largest assumed mass or cost). Novelty over prior work: low and not demonstrated; soundness: the optimiser is correct, the metric is not robust (cost artefact). No penalty is tied to a measurement, so the 'performance budget' has no unit a practitioner can verify.

defects.what: Cost closure is inflated by an accounting artefact: every printed replacement part is costed at 0.5 per unit, so printed M8 nuts (100 x 0.5 = 50) replace purchased nuts (100 x 0.03 = 3) and the whole line counts as makeable. Replacing only the M8 nut gives 33.6% cost closure as reported; costing the printed nut at the 0.03 it replaces gives 17.4% (independent script). The README attributes the jump to 'many cheap lines'.

Seeded bug in greedy(): ranking by gain times penalty instead of gain per penalty leaves all 5 tests passing. The greedy test checks only budget and that greedy does not beat exhaustive. No test pins any number in results.txt or the sensitivity analysis in run.py.

Wood-smooth-rods replaces 140 to 165 g steel rods with 30 g dowel, shrinking the mass denominator and moving the reported mass closure (28.6% at budget 1.0; 37.0% with the steel mass kept). The assumption is not stated in the README results.

Not tied to a programme and weak against prior work: the penalties are arbitrary, 2^7 search is enumerable, and Freitas and Merkle closure taxonomy and Moses and Chirikjian are not cited; nothing here is new beyond the inputs.
Package imports the sibling project by sys.path.insert (breaks as an installed package); closure_of duplicates selfrep_closure.closure.closure; run.py mutates the global SUBS list in place.

verdict: The arithmetic is right and fully reproducible: run.py regenerates results.txt byte for byte, and my independent script recovered the baseline (43.1 / 22.4 / 15.9%, 29 vitamin lines), the all-substitutions figures (60.4 / 35.8 / 47.7%, 19 lines) and the 17-of-21 greedy count. But the headline cost-closure finding is largely an accounting artefact (printed nuts costed at 0.5 each against 0.03 purchased: 33.6% reported, 17.4% if costed consistently), the dowel mass assumption moves the mass result by 8 points, a seeded bug reversing the greedy rule passed all 5 tests, and the penalties that drive every conclusion are arbitrary with no cited closure literature. Correctness, claims and verification are 2, so it does not meet the bar; it is finished (completeness 3) as a small honest toy rather than a PhD-level programme step. Recheck: `python3 experiments/run.py`, the budget-0.5 cost row, and the mutation at design.py:94. Small safe fix: cost printed parts at the cost of what they replace (or report cost closure only with that rule), add a test pinning greedy's choice at budget 1.0, and cite Freitas and Merkle.
